entries.title: UK: Iran 'highly likely' to be behind RAF Fairford incident
entries.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham told parliament there were "strong indications" of Iranian involvement. The government summoned Iran's ambassador. The scare at RAF Fairford led to the withdrawal of USAF B-1 heavy bombers.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK: Iran 'highly likely' to be behind RAF Fairford incident

October 12, 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told parliament there were "strong indications" of Iranian involvement. The government summoned Iran's ambassador. The scare at RAF Fairford led to the withdrawal of USAF B-1 heavy bombers.

The British government has accused Iran of involvement in a security alert outside a UK/US airbase in southern England last month, summoning the ambassador and announcing sanctions against two individuals. 

Five British nationals were arrested in the vicinity of the RAF Fairford airbase on September 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses. They were later released on bail under strict conditions, and another arrest followed days later.

Police had already said they were considering the possibility of a foreign state actor's involvement, not least given RAF Fairford's importance to the US Air Force as one of the European bases that handles heavy bombers like B-1's and B-52's, with ample range to reach Iran. 

What did Prime Minister Andy Burnham tell parliament?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in the House of Commons on Monday that the UK might yet put further sanctions on Iran in response.

He said there were indications of Iran coordinating the potential plot.

"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," he said. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil."

The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited.

Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the vans. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum.

"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said.

Foreign Secretary Miliband says Iranian ambassador summoned

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil."

Iran's state news agency IRNA reported Ambassador Ali Moussavi as "categorically rejecting the accusations" and calling on the British government "to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."

Miliband said that two individuals would be subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification.

He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network.

Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas."

Joint statement from 29 countries condemns 'Iran's use of violent attacks'

Shortly afterwards, a total of 29 countries issued a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks."

It said these included "the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."

All of the so-called "Five Eyes" alliance and most European NATO members were listed among the signatories, including but not limited to the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Spain and Ireland.

In the aftermath of the September 27 incident at Fairford, the high-tech US B-1 bombers left the airbase. The older and larger contingent of B-52's remained there. 

RAF Fairford is one of several airbases in southern England with a large US usage footprint. It's located around two hours' drive west of London, in a rural area north of Swindon.

As with most such bases, it can trace its roots back to the second World War when Nazi Germany occupied most of mainland Europe and Allied powers were operating air raids and preparing for the D-Day landings out of Britain.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Hundreds of French supermarkets hit by a cyberattack that defrosted refrigeration systems
entries.summary: Hundreds of French supermarkets saw their refrigeration systems defrosted, spoiling tons of frozen food. The unprecedented attack has raised serious questions about food security across Europe.
entries.content:
October 12, 2026

Hundreds of French supermarkets saw their refrigeration systems defrosted, spoiling tons of frozen food. The unprecedented attack has raised serious questions about food security across Europe.

Hundreds of French supermarkets were forced to throw away perishable goods on Monday after hackers commandeered refrigeration systems across the country, spoiling stock at major chains in a sophisticated overnight cyberattack.

Hackers destroyed the food by taking control of refrigeration systems at Cooperative U, Leclerc, Les Mousquetaires, and Intermarche stores across the country and then defrosting thousands of freezer and refrigeration units.

During the overnight attack, in some cases, fully-stocked fridges were heated up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for more than six hours.

Over 400 stores were hit according to retailers.

Prosecutors in Paris confirmed the attacks and said fires had been reported at some locations.

Intermarche said impacted stores had no choice but to "throw away all fresh and frozen products."

Leclerc told French news agency AFP that "a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," triggering "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores."

How were the refrigeration systems accessed?

The refrigeration systems targeted were reportedly from Danish supplier Danfoss, something suggested by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office, which reportedly identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor."

Danfoss said ​it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems," adding that the units in question "were running outdated firmware."

Danfoss said it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions."

Prime Minister Lecornu's office has tasked the French cybersecurity agency ANSSI with investigating the attack and is "liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected."

"Security issues" were also reported in Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, with Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize saying it had taken refrigeration systems offline to protect them, though the company added that it saw no connection to the French attacks.

Attacks on food supply now 'a reality'

It is currently unclear who could have been responsible for the cyberattack, and no group or individual has yet to claim responsibility.

The incident comes amid growing concern over vulnerabilities related to industrial ransomware and cyberattacks by malign actors in general, as well as heightened sensitivity toward Russian hybrid attacks in the midst of rising tensions over the war in Ukraine.

Last month, French President Emmanuel Macron — a strong supporter of Kyiv's self-defense against Russia — ordered measures put in place to protect France's critical infrastructure from Kremlin "hybrid attacks."

Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher, wrote on X: "Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable."

"Food security requires more attention at all levels," wrote EU Food and Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, who condemned the attack, adding that the "exploitation of food" is now a "reality."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Poland reports arrests of 2 Turkish citizens in Germany in connection with Starlink station fire last month
entries.summary: Polish authorities have reported the arrests of two Turkish citizens in Germany in connection with alleged sabotage of a Starlink station last month. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the fire an act of "hybrid warfare."
entries.content:
Poland

Poland: Germany detains 2 in connection with Starlink fire

October 12, 2026

Polish authorities have reported the arrests of two Turkish citizens in Germany in connection with alleged sabotage of a Starlink station last month. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the fire an act of "hybrid warfare."

Polish officials on Monday said that two Turkish citizens have been detained in Germany in connection with a fire last month at a Starlink station in Poland. 

The satellite-based Starlink internet service is widely used by the military of Poland's neighbor Ukraine amid the Russian invasion. 

Officials from several EU countries have been warning of mounting Russian sabotage, cyber and hybrid attacks across Europe aiming either to erode support for Ukraine or to impact Ukraine directly.

Polish officials did not specify exactly where or when the two men were allegedly detained in Germany.

What did Poland say about the arrests and the case?

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski reported the arrests on Monday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk following soon after. 

"On behalf of Polish services, German police detained two Turkish citizens suspected of setting fire to a Starlink station in Masovia," he said on social media. "This is another act of hybrid warfare. The perpetrators of the sabotage will answer before the Polish justice system."

Masovia is the province that includes the Polish capital Warsaw, not that far from Poland's eastern borders to Belarus and Ukraine.

Poland blames Russia for incident

Poland's Special Services Minister Tomasz Siemoniak alleged that Russia was behind the incident.

He also told a press conference that, "​it is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning ​to individuals linked ‌to the criminal underworld" for such attacks.

Russia typically dismisses European claims of hybrid warfare or systemic sabotage as either anti-Russian hysteria or disinformation.

entries.title: Fact check: Viral videos falsely linked to Riyadh airport attacks
entries.summary: Many videos claiming to show an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport have gone viral online. DW Fact check analyzes some of the most-shared footage and finds evidence it was created using AI.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Fact check: Fake viral videos linked to the Riyadh airport attacks

October 12, 2026

Many videos claiming to show an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport have gone viral online. DW Fact check analyzes some of the most-shared footage and finds evidence it was created using AI.

Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in recent days. At least 16 people have been killed since last Thursday, according to Saudi authorities. 

As news of the attacks spreads, social media users have been sharing videos that they claim show the strikes. While some authentic footage of the attacks and their aftermath has circulated online, DW Fact check found that several viral videos are not genuine and show signs of being AI-generated.

Claim: This post with 1.7 million views on X, claims it shows the moment of an attack on the airport. 

DW Fact check: Fake

The video has been online since March 2026 and could not show the most recent attacks on the airport. 

Hectic camera movements and blurry footage help conceal glitches that often point to AI-generated content. However, our frame-by-frame analysis identified several inconsistencies. That suggests the video was AI-generated.

In the video, people run toward an exit as an explosion occurs outside. Despite the apparent danger, they continue moving toward the blast, seemingly through a glass door. This reaction is implausible.

Around 10 seconds into the video, an image of a hand holding a smartphone appears on the side of a man's head.

At 12 seconds, one man first appears not to have a hand, then miraculously has one.

Meta's AI identification tool finds AI signatures in the video and concludes it was created using generative AI.

Many shared the video as authentic, including the Times of Israel– its post had more than 256,000 views at the time of writing. 

The video has appeared in many languages, including Arabic, English, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, Nepali, and it has been shared on YouTube, Instagram, TikTok,  Facebookand other platforms.

AI generates video from real photograph

Claim: In this post on X with 2.9 million views, a user claims it shows "new video footage of the moment King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh was targeted." 

DW Fact check: Fake

The video is AI-generated and contains several inconsistencies when compared with the real airport. Using a reverse image search, we found the photograph used to generate the fake video.

The original image was uploaded to stock photo database Shutterstockin 2016. Although it was taken from a slightly different angle it shows many visual cues that overlap with the video, including the white triangular geometric patterns of the airport building roof, the dome to the left, the luggage transport vehicles and the open and closed doors of the plane. 

Other elements are missing. In the video, the light pole to the left of the aircraft appears without any lamps attached. The video is grainy and contains some visual glitches where parts of the image suddenly become blurry.

When the supposed missile strikes the plane, a nearby vehicle significantly changes its shape as it is thrown into the air. Another inconsistency is that, despite the missile's massive explosion and a resulting fireball, nearby objects do not cast corresponding shadows.

The account that shared the video has repeatedly posted AI-generated content in the past.

Whereas the October 8 attack at King Khalid International Airport did reportedly badly damage a plane, this video does not show the moment of attack. 

Video predates attack and shows people move through objects

Claim: This TikTok postwith more than 301,000 views claims that the footage was recorded "just now from the heart of Riyadh Airport."

DW Fact check: Fake

This video had already circulated online in March 2026, months before the attack. We found the video was shared in Greek, Albanian, Turkish and Russian. 

The footage contains several visual anomalies. Parts of the image appear blurry, and some people seem to merge into one another. In addition, a row of red lights in the terminal switches on one second before the supposed explosion becomes visible through the window.

The clearest indication that the video is AI-generated is the way people move through the queue barriers. At the beginning of the video, several people appear to walk directly through them. After the supposed explosion, some individuals run straight through barriers that appear to end mid-air and are connected on only one side.

Video contains Google AI watermarks

Claim: This TikTok post, which has garnered more than 500,000 views, reports on the attacks on the airports in Riyadh and Abha and includes a compilation of videos. We examined the first video. 

DW Fact check: Fake

Analysis using Google Gemini detected that the video was generated, at least in part, with Google AI tools. The clip contains a SynthID watermark in both the images and the audio.

The same video also circulated on Facebook, where it has received more than 157,000 views. On Facebook it has been posted by an account that only shares AI-generated videos, and it is clearly labeled as "AI-content."

All four videos examined by DW Fact check are very short. Two are between six and ten seconds long, while the other two last 13 and 15 seconds, respectively. Such brief videos are easier to create with AI and often contain very little visual information, making it difficult for viewers to verify their authenticity.

Daniel Ebertz contributed to this research.

Edited by: Chiponda Chimbelu

entries.title: Germany: Labor Minister's resignation puts a spotlight on cracks within the government
entries.summary: Following the sudden resignation of Bärbel Bas as Labor Minister and co-chair of the Social Democratic Party, accusations are flying in Chancellor Merz's coalition government.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Labor Minister's resignation leaves the government in turmoil

October 12, 2026

Following the sudden resignation of Bärbel Bas as Labor Minister and co-chair of the Social Democratic Party, accusations are flying in Chancellor Merz's coalition government.

The week kicked off with a bang: On Monday morning, Bärbel Bas announced her resignation as Labor Minister and as Co-Chair of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "Following the death of my stepdaughter, I realized that I need time to come to terms with my grief," Bärbel Bas wrote in a personal statement to party members.

However, she also cited "the public attacks against me — unfortunately, including some from within the ranks of our coalition partner" as reasons for her resignation. In fact, the pressure on Bas increased significantly in recent days. The centrist coalition government is urgently awaiting key legislative proposals from the Ministry of Labor.

Before the summer recess in July, a commission had already presented comprehensive proposals for reforming Germany's statutory pension system. The coalition partners of SPD and the center-right Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) wanted these proposals to be quickly turned into legislation. To date, however, no finalized drafts have been presented.

There had been calls for Bas' resignation

"The minister is no longer tenable. For months, she has been blocking the reforms our country so urgently needs," railed Christian von Stetten, head of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group's caucus representing medium-sized enterprises, said in reference to Bas in September.

In early October, such criticism was echoed by CDU Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, who demanded that the pension reform be passed by the end of the year. Bas had to submit the bill "promptly," Reiche said, although it was known at the time what a difficult personal situation her cabinet colleague was in at the time.

SPD co-leader, Finance Minister and Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil reacted sharply on Monday, saying the political attacks against Bas had been "disgraceful."  Following a meeting of the SPD leadership, he told journalists in Berlin: "This poisons the political discourse, and — in the interest of preserving our political culture — I hope that everyone will take a step back and reflect on what has actually happened over the past few weeks." He called on all centrist politicians to be careful "that we don't destroy the good people in politics by attacking one another."

Such accusations carry significant weight at a time when the coalition is already mired in a deep crisis.

Adding to this is the new vacancy at the top of the SPD. Without Bas, Klingbeil will lead the SPD alone. A party convention will be scheduled for December or January to elect new leadership for the Social Democrats. It is not certain whether Klingbeil will run again. He received a very poor result during his last reelection as party leader.

Swift replacement of Labor Minister

Alexander Schweitzer is to succeed Bärbel Bas as Federal Minister of Labor. The former state premier of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate had previously served as that state's Minister of Labor and Social Affairs. Chancellor Friedrich Merz expressed confidence that Schweitzer's experience would ensure " good cooperation within the federal government," adding that he hoped that the pending legislative proposals "will now be quickly approved by the cabinet and can be introduced into the parliamentary process."

The chancellor refuted the accusations leveled by Bas, saying that he had never discussed personal matters with her. Friedrich Merz said he had explicitly advised Bas to take the time she needed to grieve.

Merz promises change

Mistrust between the coalition partners has increased significantly, with SPD lawmakers speaking of an increasingly toxic political climate.

For months, the CDU and SPD have been grappling with low poll numbers, disappointing election results, and disputes over key reform projects. Plans for changes to the electricity tax, the introduction of a sugar tax, the pension and the labor market reform — hardly any initiative has been able to proceed without public controversy.

Adding to this is the crisis within the chancellor's party, the CDU, which saw a historic election defeat in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September, when it even lost representation in a state parliament for the first time in history.

On Sunday and Monday, the party leadership met for a closed-door session to discuss the way forward.

They produced a four-page document which indicated a shift in priorities, putting more emphasis on social issues: affordable housing, lower electricity prices, better health care, and greater respect for citizens' lifetime achievements are mentioned in the paper. This is seen as a response to criticism that the CDU had been focusing too much on economic and regulatory issues.

The chancellor admitted that voters feel that politicians are not taking their hardships and fears of social decline seriously enough. "We have to work our way out of this slump — and get out of a crisis of confidence," Merz said. "You can't just reinvent a party overnight over a weekend, but we want to show that we're ready for change... and we have to be, given the election results."

The chancellor announced that he would lower the electricity tax for everyone — a promise he had made before the general election in 2025 but had not kept.

With the closed-door meeting paper, the CDU is also sending a signal to the SPD. Instead of a programmatic shift further to the right, it is emphasizing its traditional social values — a stance that resonates well within the Social Democrats.

The chancellor made an effort to emphasize his intention to continue with the current coalition government: "The personnel changes will not call into question the basis of the coalition agreement." He then repeated what he had recently said during a visit to Ukraine: "We need a stable federal government right now in order to remain capable of acting on the international stage."

Both CDU/CSU and SPD know that calling early elections could primarily benefit the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is leading in the polls nationwide. So despite the deep rifts, Klingbeil and Merz currently see no alternative to their coalition.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Germany news: Merz says Trump's Russia diesel deal 'out of question' for Europe
entries.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia would be "out of the question" for Germany and the EU. Meanwhile, the ruling coalition has been rocked by a major resignation.
entries.content:
Germany

Merz: Trump Russia diesel deal 'out of question' for Europe

Published October 12, 2026last updated October 12, 2026

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia would be "out of the question" for Germany and the EU. Meanwhile, the ruling coalition has been rocked by a major resignation.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

These updates are now closed. These were headlines and reports from across Germany on Monday, October 12: 

  • Merz said the order of the day was new EU sanctions on Russia not diesel deals with Russia, saying Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy 'can rely on Germany'
  • Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has accused some conservative bloc members in Saxony-Anhalt of being cowards
  • Bärbel Bas, Germany's education minister and the co-chair of the SPD, has resigned amid coalition infighting with Chancellor Merz's CDU
  • The winner of Germany's most prestigious literary peace prize has cricized the country's support of the Israeli government

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Thank you for reading

Thank you for reading

Thank you for reading our Germany news blog. We will back with more news in a fresh blog on Tuesday. Tschüss!

Skip next section Merz, Zelenskyy emphasize that Russia must spare energy grid

Merz, Zelenskyy emphasize that Russia must spare energy grid

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke by telephone and agreed that Russia must agree to a mutual ceasefire regarding attacks on energy infrastructure.

According to German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius, Zelenskyy informed Merz about the significant Russian attacks on civilian targets and Ukrainian energy facilities that occurred over the weekend. Merz reaffirmed Germany's solidarity with Ukraine.

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced on his Truth Social platform that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, effective "immediately."

However, Ukrainian authorities subsequently reported targeted strikes on the power grid in Kyiv and Kharkiv.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: German labor minister's resignation leaves the government in turmoil

IN DEPTH: German labor minister's resignation leaves the government in turmoil

Following the sudden resignation of Bärbel Bas as Labor Minister and co-chair of the Social Democratic Party, accusations are flying in Chancellor Merz's coalition government.

Skip next section Police probe misuse of robot to sexually harass teenage girl

Police probe misuse of robot to sexually harass teenage girl

Police in Cologne say they are investigating the suspected use of a remote-controlled robot to sexually harass a 16-year-old girl over the weekend. 

Police said the red and gold droid led to a police operation late on Saturday night on Cologne's ring road, allegedly as two young men were trying to get attention on social media.

"The gadget is alleged to have touched a 16-year-old [girl] on the posterior and to have bumped up against her rear end" more than once, police wrote.

"The 16-year-old [male] owner of the robot and his 19-year-old companion are suspected of filming the suspected assault, streaming it live online and providing commentary," police said.

The incident took place outside a fast food restaurant shortly before midnight.

Police arrived soon after and found robot inside the trunk or boot of a Volkswagen, saying that the 16-year-old owner had stowed it there prior to their arrival.

"How the robot was operating at the time of the crime and whether somebody was steering it with intent is now the subject of a criminal police investigation," police said, adding that they had seized both the robot and two of the suspects' phones.

Skip next section New bridge opens at Danevirke Museum in Schleswig Holstein

New bridge opens at Danevirke Museum in Schleswig Holstein

German and Danish local politicians attended the ribbon cutting on Monday for a new pedestrian bridge near the town of Schleswig at the UNESCO heritage site the archaeological border complex of Hedeby and Danevirke (or Haithabu und Danewerk).

The new steel bridge links the walking path along the 11th century defenses of Danish King Valdemar's Wall with an artillery firing position engineered for Danish troops in the German-Danish war of 1864.

Valdemar's Wall was one of the earliest and largest secular brickwork structures of its time, built to defend the Danish kingdom from raids from Slavic and Saxon tribes.

Known as "Schanze 14" or "Entrenchment 14," the nearby elevated platform was built in 1864 to provide a good vantage point and natural terrain-based cover for Danish artillery fighting against Prussian troops in the Second Schleswig War.

Southern Schleswig, with a majority German population, forms part of the northermost state of Schlewsig-Holstein, while Northern Schleswig is in Denmark. The age-old disputes over the territory were largely settled in a 1955 treaty assuring minority rights on either side of the border.

Skip next section German fighter jets to take part in NATO nuclear drill

German fighter jets to take part in NATO nuclear drill

Germany is sending three Tornado fighter jets to Italy to take part in NATO's annual nuclear deterrence exercise, Steadfast Noon, which begins on Tuesday.

The aircraft, normally stationed at Büchel air base in western Germany, have been deployed to Aviano Air Base in northern Italy, a German Air Force spokesperson told the DPA news agency.

Several dozen German military personnel will also participate in the exercise, which rehearses NATO's ability to deploy nuclear weapons in the event of a conflict.

No live nuclear weapons will be used. NATO says the exercise is routine, unrelated to current world events and not directed against any particular country.

The alliance has not disclosed details of this year's scenario. Last year's exercise involved around 2,000 personnel and more than 70 aircraft.

Germany participates in NATO's nuclear-sharing arrangements, under which German aircraft could deliver US nuclear weapons in a conflict.

Skip next section Germany's Merz slams Trump's Russian diesel deal

Germany's Merz slams Trump's Russian diesel deal

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has criticized US President Donald Trump's agreement to import Russian diesel, calling for tougher sanctions on Moscow instead.

"We take note of the agreement between the United States and Russia on diesel exports," Merz said in Berlin on Monday. "For Germany and Europe, such a decision is out of the question."

Merz said Russia would only negotiate seriously under pressure and called for further sanctions following Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure.

He also questioned Trump's announcement of an immediate halt to Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's energy facilities, saying Moscow had responded with massive strikes.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's announcement of the partial ceasefire came as news to him, while the Kremlin has not confirmed that it has taken effect.

Merz reaffirmed Germany's support for Ukraine and said efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace would be discussed at this week's EU summit.

Skip next section Tennis: Alexander Zverev will be world number 1 for the first time

Tennis: Alexander Zverev will be world number 1 for the first time

The long-awaited mathematical confirmation has arrived: Germany's Alexander Zverez will take the top spot in the men's singles tennis rankings at the end of the year.

A shock straight set defeat for Carlos Alcaraz on Monday in Shanghai against unseeded Belgian player Zizou Bergs made Zverev claiming the number 1 ranking innevitable.

Aged 29, Zverev will be the oldest player ever to take over the top spot for the first time in his career.

He said that knowing he'd finish the season at number was a "dream come true," and said he'd concentrate on finishing the season "in style."

It's been a year of breakthroughs for Zverev, whose career to date had long seen him living in the shadows of greats like Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, and later Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz.

He won his first two Majors, at the French Open and then the US Open, and was also runner-up to Sinner at Wimbledon. 

Sinner has not played since that final because of injury. Coupled with some patchy form from Alcaraz, this opened the door for Zverev to push to overtake them in the annual rankings.

The last — and only — German man to top tennis' world rankings was Boris Becker, who had two brief mid-season stints at number 1 in 1991. He did not finish the year as number 1, though.

Angelique Kerber also spent a combined seven and a half months at women's singles number 1 across three stints between 2016 and 2017, including at the end of the 2016 campaign. Steffi Graf meanwhile dominated the women's rankings for much of the period between 1987 and 1997.

Skip next section SPD, Greens and Left party begin coalition talks in Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania

SPD, Greens and Left party begin coalition talks in Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania

The Social Democrats (SPD) have opened up coalition talks with the Greens and the Left party in Germany's northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania, sources confirmed to local media.

The three parties have already held exploratory discussions on working together and received permission from party leadership bodies to move forward.

This comes several weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came in first in the state election with 38.2% of the vote. However, without an outright majority and no other parties willing to work with them, they were unable to form a government.

Together the SPD, Greens and Left will hold 32 seats in the 71-member state parliament, giving them three more seats than the AfD.

The regional party leaders, including incumbent SPD state premier Manuela Schwesig, are expected to issue a joint statement later today.

The trio faces a tight turnaround to secure a coalition agreement, as the state's new parliament will sit for the first time on October 20, after which there is a four-week deadline to hold an election for premier.

Skip next section Klingbeil cancels India trip, calls for SPD leadership vote

Klingbeil cancels India trip, calls for SPD leadership vote

Vice-Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has nixed a planned trip to India, saying that the Social Democrats need to hold a new vote for party leadership.

His announcement came shortly after the resignation of his party co-chair Bärbel Bas.

Klingbeil did not say whether he would run again, but confirmed that the rest of the party's top officials agreed the election was necessary.

Skip next section Wadephul hails EU Russia sanctions

Wadephul hails EU Russia sanctions

German Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul praised an "unprecedented sanctions blow" the European Union has levelled against Moscow.

"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said in a statement.

On Monday, EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.

It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.

"We are increasing the pressure until Putin is ready to negotiate seriously about peace in Ukraine," Wadephul said, though he missed the Luxembourg meeting to participate in a CDU party summit in Berlin.

Skip next section Frankfurt Book fair prize winner criticizes Germany's stance on Israel

Frankfurt Book fair prize winner criticizes Germany's stance on Israel

Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands accepted the prestigious Peace Price presented every year at the Frankfurt Book Fair, the premiere event of the German publishing industry.

Presdent Frank-Walter Steinmeier praised Sands as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."

A professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, Sands used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany's "inappropiate silence" on the Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.

"It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth," he said of the government's behavior.

You can read more about Sands and his speech here.

Skip next section Cologne teenager badly injured while 'trainsurfing'

Cologne teenager badly injured while 'trainsurfing'

Public broadcaster WDR has said that 14-year-old was badly injured on Sunday night in Cologne after engaging in "trainsurfing," or attempting to ride on the top of a moving train.

The boy is reportedly fighting for his life at a local hospital after being struck by a powerful electrical current moving between the train and the overhead wires that power it. Authorities believe he could have been hit by 15,000 volts.

Trainsurfing is, of course, illegal, and still uncommon. However, authorities are worried that social media videos may encourage young people to attempt the dangerous stunt.

Skip next section Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'

Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'

"Do you want to go somewhere else? Then just say so," Bavarian leader Markus Söder said during an interview with public broadcaster ARD. 

As a member of the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), Söder was referencing bloc members in the state of Saxony-Anhalt who are believed to have voted for a member of the far-right in a secret ballot.

Last week, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — whose chapter in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as right-wing extremist — was elected state parliamentary speaker.

This marked the first time the AfD has seen a member elected to such a position, and the first time in postwar Germany that a right-wing extremist has risen to this rank.

The populist BSW party had declared their intention to support Rausch's nomination alongside the AfD, but his win with 48 votes means that other lawmakers must have voted for him too. It is strongly suspected that these were members of the conservative CDU.

Rausch's election prompted outrage across Germany, including from CDU members who have accused their colleagues of abandoning the so-called "firewall" — the agreement amongst the country's mainstream parties not to support the AfD.

Söder called it "pretty poor form," from the CDU members in Saxony-Anhalt, saying they should "at least have the backbone" to make their decision public.

Skip next section Labor minister and SPD co-chair Bärbel Bas resigns

Labor minister and SPD co-chair Bärbel Bas resigns

Citing "open attacks" by members of senior coalition partners the CDU, Bärbel Bas has stepped down as co-leader of the SPD and as federal labor minister.

She also said a recent death in the family had influenced her decision to resign.

You can read our full report on the latest trial for Chancellor Merz's coalition here.

entries.title: US federal agents search home of Trump critic Ilhan Omar
entries.summary: Justice Department officials said the Washington residence of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, an outspoken opponent of President Trump, was raided as "part of an ongoing federal investigation."
entries.content:
United States of America

US federal agents search home of Trump critic Ilhan Omar

October 12, 2026

Justice Department officials said the Washington residence of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, an outspoken opponent of President Trump, was raided as "part of an ongoing federal investigation."

US federal agents searched the home of a Democratic congresswoman and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump on Monday, the Department of Justice (DoJ) confirmed.

Officials from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US immigration enforcement, were seen early on Monday morning outside the Washington home of Ilhan Omar.

"Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice," a DoJ spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in a statement which didn't specifically name Omar.

"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation."

Who is Ilhan Omar?

Omar, who came to the United States from Somalia as a child, was first elected to Congress in 2018 and is a member of the group of left-wing Democratic lawmakers known as "The Squad," who have been among Trump's most vocal opponents.

Omar represents a district including Minneapolis, home to one of the largest Somali communities in the US – a community which Trump has frequently targeted in racist outbursts.

He ​previously called Somalis "garbage" and said in February that Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from."

Last ​week, Trump called Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan Abdul El Sayed a "RADICAL Extremist" and "Terrorist Sympathizer" while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers

Democrats decry 'abuse of power'

House Democratic leaders condemned the search as an "abuse of power" by the Trump administration.

Omar said she will “not be silenced” and called the search of her home the “latest escalation” in President Donald Trump’s '‘intimidation" campaign.

Omar has called Trump's focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession" said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes ⁠to "hateful political rhetoric" especially ​from Trump.

On Monday, Omar said she will "not be silenced" and called the search of her home the "latest escalation" in Trump's "intimidation" campaign.

No charges against Omar were announced in connection with Monday's search, but US media reported that the operation was linked to a criminal fraud investigation into immigration paperwork submitted on her behalf by her late father when she was a child.

The search comes just three weeks before midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans will be trying to defend their thin majorities in the US.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?
entries.summary: The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.
entries.content:
Published October 12, 2026last updated October 12, 2026

The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.

At less than 3 centimeters (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.

In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.

What we know so far

All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."

That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.

Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.

This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.

The risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules."

That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.

Fortunately many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.

It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.

What are lung nodules?

Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.

Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.

Causes and symptoms of lung nodules

Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.

At more than 3 centimeters, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.

Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.

What makes lung nodules cancerous?

It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.

At 2 milimeters or smaller, the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 milimeters.

The risk of cancer becomes 9%-10% at about 8 to 10 milimeters. And at larger than 1 centimeter, the risk of cancer is about 15%.

The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.

There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.

According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."

Lung nodules and lung cancer are common

It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.

A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."

However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.

Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Starlink India launch: Why Elon Musk is still waiting
entries.summary: Despite securing key approvals, the Starlink satellite internet service remains in regulatory limbo, raising questions about security clearances, competition and India’s investment climate.
entries.content:
India

Starlink India launch: Why Elon Musk is still waiting

October 12, 2026

Despite securing key approvals, the Starlink satellite internet service remains in regulatory limbo, raising questions about security clearances, competition and India’s investment climate.

Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, has escalated his criticism of the delay in launching Starlink in India. Last week, he sarcastically referred to Mukesh Ambani, one of India's richest people and chairman of Reliance Industries, as "Prime Minister Ambani" and accused his supporters of protecting a monopoly.  

"Would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?" Musk wrote on X, arguing that the service could bring internet access to underserved communities across India.

Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, joined the discussion, writing: "Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy." Musk replied: "Thank you, Rahul. This is indeed troubling."

A delayed launch and a war of words

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) accused Gandhi of championing Musk's interests, while party leaders defended the government's handling of the issue.

Speaking during the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi last week, Reliance Jio chairman Akash Ambani declined to comment on Musk's remarks. He said: "I have no comments to make. We want to keep our heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."

Akash, Mukesh Ambani's eldest son, also noted that Jio was progressing on its own end-to-end indigenous satellite broadband technology stack.

Meanwhile, Starlink — despite securing key approvals and signing distribution agreements with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel — has yet to begin commercial operations in India.

Its low-earth-orbit satellites could provide internet access in remote villages, hilly regions and border areas where fiber-optic networks and mobile towers are expensive to build.

But the service would enter a market where mobile data is inexpensive and established telecom operators have extensive networks.

India's Ministry of Communications says security assessments for all three licensed satellite operators are under way and that they are at broadly the same regulatory stage.

In a statement, the ministry said every licensee must meet security conditions intended to protect users and their data. Once an assessment is completed, an operator can seek spectrum assignment. It described allegations that the framework was unfair or discriminatory as "baseless and misconceived."

Legitimate security concerns?

Starlink secured a satellite communications licence from the Department of Telecommunications and authorization from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center in 2025. These approvals do not automatically permit commercial operations, however.

The security debate surrounding Starlink has intensified following remarks by BJP leader Nishikant Dubey, who chairs a parliamentary committee. In a post on X on October 11, Dubey said the panel had examined Starlink's security challenges.

"As the chairman of the parliamentary committee, our committee has understood the challenges facing the country's security agencies through Starlink," he wrote in Hindi.

Responding to Musk's criticism, Dubey added, "India is a healthy democratic, sovereign nation, and it does not change its security policy under pressure from social media or external figures."

Dubey did not specify the security risks or regulatory requirements holding up the launch.

Former intelligence officer and national security expert Yashovardhan Jha Azad said the impasse reflected commercial competition, regulatory uncertainty and legitimate security concerns.

"The central question is: who retains effective control over an essential communications service during a crisis?" Azad told DW.

He said India needed safeguards covering traffic routing, lawful interception under due process and cybersecurity.

"The existence of security requirements, however, does not establish why Starlink's application remains pending," Azad said. He pointed out that the government has not publicly detailed which specific conditions, if any, the company still needs to satisfy.

Investment, manufacturing and affordability

The delay in Starlink's launch has raised questions about the predictability of India's investment environment.

Economist Lekha Chakrabarty, who has studied the issue closely, said the problem was not that India was shutting its doors to foreign investment, but that companies could not plan around an open-ended approval process.

"The Starlink impasse is best read not as India closing its door to foreign investment, but as a failure to make an already open door predictably passable," Chakrabarty told DW.

She said security reviews were necessary given the sensitivity of satellite communications, which involve critical infrastructure, cross-border data, gateway control and lawful interception.

But the problem, she said, was the lack of transparency around approval criteria and timelines.

"Investors can price known rules, they cannot efficiently price discretionary, multi-agency processes with uncertain endpoints," Chakrabarty added.

Pankaj Mohindroo, chairman of the India Cellular and Electronics Association, said Starlink's entry could create opportunities for Indian electronics manufacturers in satellite terminals, antennas, communication modules and network equipment.

"India already has a strong trusted electronics manufacturing base, which provides an opportunity for global technology companies to develop local partnerships and strengthen domestic supply chains," he told DW.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat over North Korean POWs?
entries.summary: Seoul and Kyiv are trading accusations after the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea. The South insists the move was to be kept secret as it seeks to avoid antagonizing Pyongyang.
entries.content:
South Korea

Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat?

October 12, 2026

Seoul and Kyiv are trading accusations after the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea. The South insists the move was to be kept secret as it seeks to avoid antagonizing Pyongyang.

South Korea's ambassador to Kyiv returned to Seoul on Saturday, his recall the latest in a series of tit-for-tat actions that have severely strained bilateral ties.

The sudden deterioration in their relationship can be traced back to September 23, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.

The soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in the Russian Kursk region in January 2025 as they fought alongside Russian troops.

The South Korean government immediately expressed its anger at Zelenskyy's revelation, insisting that the two governments had reached an agreement to keep the transfer of the two men in mid-September a secret.

Kyiv hit back, by saying that no confidentiality agreement had been in place, to which South Korea accused Ukraine of effectively lying and demanded an official explanation and an apology.

Ukraine has attempted to smooth over what it has called a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of the public apology that was expected in Seoul.

Then, reports emerged last week that a close adviser to Zelenskyy had said that more than 176,000 tons of diesel and other energy products were shipped to Russia from South Korean ports in July and August of this year, which would be a breach of international sanctions.

The office of president Lee Jae Myung in Seoul denied the accusation, and two days later recalled its ambassador to Kyiv.

What is behind Seoul's need for secrecy?

There are several reasons why South Korea wanted to keep the POW transfer secret, Erwin Tan, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University, told DW.

"The first was that revealing that the POWs had been repatriated to South Korea would result in Pyongyang retaliating against the families of the men for surrendering," Tan said.

"Seoul also wanted to maintain a channel for communication with Pyongyang," Tan said. "This is a major consideration for the left-leaning wing of Korean politics, which includes President Lee and has historically favored seeking rapprochement with the North."

Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, agrees that the South Korean government wanted to avoid "friction" with the North.

But Kim pointed out that it was always very likely that both Moscow and Pyongyang would find out about the transfer sooner or later and that Lee was being criticized in some quarters at home for appearing weak.

"There is criticism that Lee's administration is effectively appeasing the North, that it has become too soft, and that is a very worrisome situation," Kim said. Yet he admits to being surprised at how quickly the issue escalated.

"I think Lee was very angry that he was publicly being accused of lying about the agreement and it rapidly grew into a very messy confrontation," he said.

Has Zelenskyy's approach backfired?

While it is unclear why Zelenskyy used his high-profile UN speech to announce the repatriation of the two POWs, Kim believes it may have been a calculated move to win more support from Seoul.

Kyiv could have carried out a prisoner swap with the Russians and won the freedom of some of its own men in return.

But, Kim pointed out, Ukraine instead chose to accede to Seoul's request in the hope that South Korea would respond with additional financial and possibly even military support. That move appears to have backfired.

Professor Tan anticipates that the two governments will continue to "vent steam" over the issue.

"Given the high profile nature of the mutual accusations, both sides will probably engage in a mutual blame game for the immediate future, but I doubt that it will turn into a long-term case of mutual acrimony," he said.

"I anticipate that after the furor has died down and the press is looking for the next new story, both sides will quietly resume contact on the basis of mutual pragmatism."

Edited by: Karl Sexton
